Interesting. Didn't see it that way before (then again, the first time I read this story was a sci-fi'ed version by Fred Saberhagen (called The Graphic of Dorian Gray). Read (okay, skimmed) the original (and viewed the black and white movie) and thought it was pretty neat.

I took a psychoanalytical approach to this novel, and compared the characters to aesthetic theories of art. Basically, I read Dorian to be literal artwork, who at the beginning held a predetermined affinity for romanticism, set into motion by the artist, Basil Hallward.

Hallward sees the beauty within Dorian and projects unto him a distinctly Romantic aestheticism. Keep in mind that one of the maxims of Romanticism is that true beauty lies beneath the form. For example, when a Romantic painter creates a portrait of nature, he is attempting to capture the immense, unadulterated beauty that lies beneath its form. That is why, when the artist paints Dorian, and it turns out to be the most beautiful painting he's ever seen, the portrait reflects Dorian's beauty.

When Hallward plans to introduce Dorian to Lord Henry Wotton, he begs of him not to corrupt the boy. As we quickly learn, Wotton is a despicably sardonic character that emulates the moral hypocrisy of Victorian Society; he is the personification of the aesthetic philosophy know as Hedonism. You can perceive this transference to be the transition between two aesthetic schools of thought, as the Romantic Era gives way to more perverse conceptions of art through culture.

As Dorian assumes the corrupt, hedonistic philosophies of Wotton, we now see the degredation of art as it plays through the life of Dorian Gray--and the hideously moribund painting ironically represents the beauty behind the art.
